Vale and Shandong Shipping Corporation recently concluded an agreement for new ethanol-powered Guaibamax vessels, which are scheduled for delivery starting in 2029.

The agreement marked an unprecedented milestone for global iron ore transport: this is the first time in the maritime industry that ethanol will be used as the primary fuel on an ocean-going vessel.

Ethanol has the potential to reduce carbon emissions by around 90% compared to the use of heavy fuel oil, commonly used in shipping.

The agreement between Vale and Shandong includes 25-year contracts for the construction of two vessels, with an option for additional ships.

The adoption of these second-generation Guaibamax vessels, which are 340 meters long and have a capacity of 325,000 tonnes, is part of the Brazilian mining company’s multi-fuel strategy.

In addition to ethanol, these vessels will be capable of using methanol and heavy fuel oil, and their design also allows for conversion to use liquefied natural gas (LNG) or ammonia.

“Vale’s pioneering efforts towards decarbonization in maritime transport are guided by a strategy that combines flexibility and efficiency. The use of ethanol as fuel in the ships that transport our ore, combined with the adoption of rotor sails to harness wind energy, places Vale in a unique position for the energy transition in global shipping over the coming decades, whilst driving similar initiatives in the sector,” said Rodrigo Bermelho, Vale’s Director of Shipping.

Considering the full fuel cycle from well to wake, ethanol can reduce carbon emissions by around 90% (in the case of second-generation ethanol) compared with heavy fuel oil. In addition to maritime transport, Vale’s adoption of ethanol in its logistics operations includes trials on trucks at its operations and on locomotives on the Vitória a Minas Railway (EFVM).

The new ethanol-powered ships will be similar to 10 other methanol dual-fuel vessels that Shandong will deliver to Vale from 2027 onwards.

The second generation of the Guaibamax will be equipped with five rotor sails – which harnesses wind energy to reduce fuel consumption – more efficient engines, hydrodynamic devices, a shaft generator, frequency inverters and silicone paint, amongst other energy efficiency improvements. The set of technologies applied will reduce GHG emissions by around 15% compared to the current generation of Guaibamax.

These technologies and alternative fuels are being tested as part of the Ecoshipping program, a research and development initiative created by Vale to support the maritime industry’s decarbonisation efforts and improve the efficiency of the mining company’s fleet.

title: Global study reveals wind propulsion can cut fleet-wide emissions but only with stronger policy action
description:
Until now, no study has assessed the decarbonization potential of wind propulsion across the entire maritime fleet.
Bulk carriers and tankers first: The top 17% of vessels, predominantly bulk carriers and tankers, deliver 50% of total emissions savings.
Policy is the bottleneck, not technology: Without stronger incentives, wind propulsion delivers only 0.2% emissions reduction by 2050.
Wind propulsion is not a future option; it’s a solution we can deploy today.
This study shows wind propulsion is ready to play a major role, but only if policy is designed to reward those who act early and act genuinely.
text:
Until now, no study has assessed the decarbonization potential of wind propulsion across the entire maritime fleet. This study addresses that gap and the findings are clear: wind propulsion is a commercially available, proven technology capable of delivering real emissions reductions today, before next-generation fuels become widely available or affordable.

Based on modeling of main engine emissions across the global fleet by the Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research in Manchester, UK, wind propulsion could reduce annual CO₂ by 7.8% by 2050. That is the equivalent to removing up to 170 million cars from the road every year. But the speed of policy ambition will reflect the scale of impact, with potential CO₂ savings of up to 762 million tonnes by 2050.

Key findings

Significant, well-evidenced savings: Drawing on 1.74 billion km of real voyage data, wind propulsion can cut fleet-wide fuel use by 6.3–9.4%. These are conservative estimates; the true potential is greater when operational optimization is applied, such as weather routing, slow steaming, hull optimization for new-build vessels and primary wind designs.

Bulk carriers and tankers first: The top 17% of vessels, predominantly bulk carriers and tankers, deliver 50% of total emissions savings. Targeted policy support for these ship types can unlock disproportionate near-term gains.

Reducing pressure on future fuel supply chains: Every tonne of fuel avoided through wind propulsion eases constraints on scarce e-fuel production, supports a more equitable transition, and allows renewable electricity to serve priority uses first.

Policy is the bottleneck, not technology: Without stronger incentives, wind propulsion delivers only 0.2% emissions reduction by 2050. The IMO's Net-Zero Framework must reward real, early reductions and limit the use of trading mechanisms as a substitute for genuine progress. At the same time, strengthening/tightening the Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) is critical to encourage the installation of wind-assisted propulsion systems

Waiting is not a strategy: Decarbonization goals set out in the International Maritime Organization (IMO)’s greenhouse gas strategy are coming up fast: 30% emission reduction by 2030, 80% by 2040, and fully decarbonized by 2050. Most ships operating in the 2030s are already in service. Retrofitting them now builds skills, supply chains, and momentum while locking in real cumulative reductions during the critical decade ahead. It also directly supports the IMO’s commitment to at least 5% - striving for 10% - uptake of zero- or near-zero-emission technologies, fuels, and energy sources by 2030.

Anaïs Rios, Senior Shipping Policy Officer, Seas At Risk, says, "The ships needed to reach 2030 climate targets are already at sea, and they can be powered by wind. Retrofitting sails cuts fuel use and emissions now, while alternative fuels remain decades away from being available at scale. Wind propulsion is not a future option; it’s a solution we can deploy today. The priority is to scale it up and ensure the transition is fair and accessible to all.”

Dr James Mason, Research Associate, Tyndall Centre for Climate Change Research at the University of Manchester, says, “This is the most comprehensive study undertaken to date on how wind propulsion can scale up and contribute to decarbonizing the maritime fleet. Using advanced modeling techniques and real operational data, we have shown that a targeted deployment on top-performing vessels can provide meaningful CO2 savings. If scale up of the technology is supported over the next critical decade, wind propulsion could play a vital role in reducing cumulative emissions and limiting the maritime sector’s contribution to ever-worsening climate change impacts.”

Policy recommendations

For wind propulsion to deliver its full potential, IMO and EU policy frameworks must be structured to reward real, early emission reductions. As the IMO is about to restart global decarbonization negotiations, Seas At Risk calls for:

Real, verified savings recognized: Fuel and emissions savings must be fully reflected in ships' GHG performance, including through the IMO’s Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII), so that wind-assisted vessels see a clear improvement in carbon intensity ratings.

Action is more attractive than paying: *Remedial units must be priced at a level that invests in real solutions, such as wind propulsion, consistently more attractive than purchasing compliance.

Flexibility mechanisms must not replace real progress: Limits on **Surplus Unit trading are essential to ensure each ship retains a clear incentive to reduce its own emissions, rather than buying its way to compliance.

Revenues for immediate solutions: Funds must support retrofit technologies such as wind propulsion, operational optimization—such as vessel speed reduction and weather routing —and capacity building, with particular attention to enabling access in developing countries, especially SIDS and LDCs, to support a more equitable transition.

Shipping pollution is global. So is responsibility. The IMO's Net-Zero Framework represents a critical opportunity to move from ambition to action. This study shows wind propulsion is ready to play a major role, but only if policy is designed to reward those who act early and act genuinely.

text:
Hong Kong-listed Pacific Basin Shipping is tweaking its fleet renewal strategy, scrapping near-term dual-fuel orders in favour of conventional tonnage while keeping optionality for greener ships later in the decade.

The dry bulk owner said it has terminated earlier agreements for four 64,000 dwt dual-fuel ultramax newbuildings and replaced them with contracts for four conventionally fuelled vessels at a total cost of $156.8m, or $39.2m each. The ships will be built in Japan by Nihon Shipyard with deliveries slated between 2028 and mid-2029.

The company has also secured an option to order two methanol dual-fuel ultramaxes for $91m in total, with delivery slots stretching into 2030–2031.

The shift reflects growing uncertainty around the timing and structure of global decarbonisation rules, particularly after the International Maritime Organization failed to finalise its net-zero framework last year.

Chief executive Martin Fruergaard said the move trims near-term capital exposure while keeping the company flexible as regulation evolves.

“Converting to conventional vessels is a financially prudent response to the current uncertainty around green fuel regulation,” he said, adding that modern, fuel-efficient designs remain central to the company’s strategy.

Alongside the ultramax reshuffle, Pacific Basin is also doubling down on the smaller end of the fleet. The owner has lifted its handysize newbuilding programme in China from four to six ships, placing two additional 40,000 dwt orders at Jiangmen Nanyang Ship Engineering for a combined $59.6m.

The vessels will share the same fuel-efficient, open-hatch design as the four units ordered in late 2025 and are due for delivery in the second half of 2028.

text:
Reducing methane slip

Methane slip remains a key issue for ships that use LNG, but dual-fuel engine makers have been making advances in reducing the amount of unburned methane that escapes through the ship’s exhaust. Improvements in lowering methane slip and the greenhouse gas intensity of LNG come primarily through high-pressure diesel cycle technology and aftertreatment systems.

Lowering so-called fugitive methane emissions, including methane slip, is critical from both an environmental compliance and fuel efficiency perspective. Methane has a global warming potential 28 times that of CO2 over a 100-year timeframe and more than 80 times the CO2 intensity over the first 20 years of its presence in the atmosphere.

For operators looking to improve energy efficiency and save money, unburned methane equates to higher fuel consumption, higher opex, and higher taxes under UK and EU emissions schemes. Reducing slip now will mean lower fuel costs when using more expensive bioLNG and synthetic LNG.

But the biggest sources of fugitive methane emissions for the LNG supply chain – production and distribution – fall outside of the scope of engine makers’ work.

LR points out that there are real benefits to improving current production and distribution through less carbon-intensive processes and lowering fugitive methane emissions, but that a transition to ’cleaner’ forms of LNG is needed to achieve deeper emissions reductions in the longer term.

“Already today, green liquefaction can reduce GHG emissions involved in LNG production by 10%. But in the longer term, cleaner LNG means developing the production and supply of methane from renewable sources, giving shipping access to far deeper GHG emissions reduction potential from LNG as a fuel,” said the class society.

“Crucially, regulators will need to acknowledge these supply chain improvements if they are to stimulate uptake of cleaner LNG,” added LR.

EU Renewable Energy Directive default values for fuels

The EU’s Renewable Energy Directive contains typical and default values for the GHG emissions savings from a range of biofuels by feedstock, against a fossil comparator of 94 g CO₂ eq/MJ, assuming no net carbon emissions from land-use change.

According to the report, there is a “wide range in the GHG intensity of biomethane, depending on the feedstock used, production process, and other factors.”

Using current default values, the report breaks down the GHG savings default values of biomethane production by feedstock and technological options.

Wet manure provides the best GHG emissions savings default values over the wide range of technological production options, ranging from a high of 202% to a low of 72%.

Further methane slip reductions needed

LR does make it clear that LNG fuel’s long-term emissions-reduction credentials rely on its GHG lifecycle analysis and reducing methane slip across the entire LNG value chain – from production to shipping to combustion.

The timing of the announcement of the release of the 47-page report, Fuel for Thought: LNG for Cruise, coincided with the cruise industry’s biggest players gathering this week in Miami for Seatrade Global Cruise 2026 to celebrate a year of exceptional growth and a record-breaking orderbook. Last year, 37M passengers travelled on cruise ships, and the value of the newbuilding orderbook is set to surpass US$100Bn.

LNG is the most widely adopted alternative fuel for cruise ships, with some 30 ships in service – just under 10% of the global fleet (20,000 gt and above). The current orderbook includes 29 LNG-fuelled ships, six methanol-fuelled ships, and two hydrogen-capable ships.

“For cruise operators, the report positions LNG not as an end point, but as a practical enabler of the industry’s decarbonisation pathway,” said LR global passenger ship segment vice president Francesco Ruiso.

The report examines the full lifecycle performance of LNG, including well-to-wake emissions, regulatory treatment under IMO and EU regimes, and the economic implications of emerging compliance mechanisms such as the IMO Net Zero Framework and FuelEU Maritime.

Cruise Lines International Association president and chief executive Bud Darr said his members are investing in environmental technology to decarbonise their ships and “have the backing of the banking community to do that.”

During the keynote session at Seatrade Cruise Global, Mr Darr said that his members are still committed to achieving net zero by 2050, “even though the regulatory environment is very confused about it. We’re still moving forward, but we’ve got to have the fuels, and we really need to have a serious commitment to make that happen.”

text:
Executive Summary

The global maritime industry stands at an inflection point. Responsible for approximately 3% of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions — equivalent to the total annual output of Japan — international shipping faces unprecedented regulatory, commercial, and reputational pressure to decarbonize. The International Maritime Organization's (IMO) Net-Zero Framework, approved in April 2025 and targeted for entry into force in 2027-2028, will for the first time impose binding, well-to-wake GHG fuel intensity reductions on ocean-going ships above 5,000 gross tonnage, a fleet segment representing 85% of sectoral emissions.

Into this landscape, the United States biofuels industry — encompassing corn and cellulosic ethanol, soy and waste-based biodiesel, renewable diesel, and bio-LNG — brings unmatched scale, established infrastructure, and competitive cost structures. Simultaneously, a new generation of US companies in green hydrogen, low-carbon ammonia, e-methanol, e-ammonia, and carbon capture are positioning to serve the longer-term needs of a zero-emission fleet.

This monograph provides a comprehensive analysis of each fuel pathway's technological profile, GHG reduction potential, infrastructure readiness, and cost competitiveness. It profiles the leading US companies that could supply the global marine industry. It argues that the near-to-medium term opportunity — through at least 2038 — belongs principally to biofuels, which offer proven emission reductions of 60-90%, drop-in compatibility with existing engines and infrastructure, and commercially competitive pricing. The longer-term, post-2035 transition will require massive scaling of e-fuels and green ammonia, for which US producers are investing now. Carbon capture serves as a bridge and accelerant across all time horizons.

1. The Maritime Decarbonization Imperative

1.1 Scale of the Challenge

International shipping moves approximately 90% of world trade by volume, carrying everything from raw materials and foodstuffs to finished goods and energy commodities. The industry has historically been one of the least regulated large emitters, benefiting from cheap, energy-dense heavy fuel oil (HFO) — among the dirtiest refined petroleum products. HFO's low cost has been a cornerstone of global trade competitiveness, but its environmental costs are stark: high sulfur content, fine particulate matter, black carbon, and significant CO2, methane, and nitrous oxide emissions.

The maritime sector currently consumes roughly 300 million tonnes of fuel annually, generating approximately 1 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent each year. Without intervention, these emissions are projected to grow substantially by 2050 as global trade volumes expand.

1.2 The IMO Regulatory Architecture

The IMO has constructed an increasingly ambitious regulatory scaffold. Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) requirements for new ships have been in place since 2013. Carbon Intensity Indicators (CII) and the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) entered mandatory effect in January 2023. The pivotal step came in July 2023 when MEPC 80 adopted the revised IMO GHG Strategy: net-zero emissions "by or around 2050," with checkpoint targets of at least 20-30% total GHG reduction by 2030 and 70% by 2040 versus 2008 baselines. Zero- or near-zero-emission fuels must supply at least 5% — striving for 10% — of shipping energy by 2030.

This strategy was translated into binding regulation at MEPC 83 in April 2025, where the IMO approved the Net-Zero Framework (NZF). The NZF establishes two interlocking instruments: a GHG Fuel Intensity (GFI) standard measured on a well-to-wake lifecycle basis in gCO2eq/MJ, ratcheting down annually from a 2028 baseline; and a financial compliance mechanism where ships exceeding GFI thresholds purchase Remedial Units at $100/tonne CO2eq (Tier 1) or $380/tonne CO2eq (Tier 2 for higher emitters). Ships that outperform the direct compliance target earn tradeable Surplus Units. Following disagreements at the October 2025 extraordinary MEPC session, formal adoption was deferred to 2026, with entry into force anticipated in 2027 and compliance beginning January 1, 2028.

The EU's FuelEU Maritime regulation, which entered force in January 2025, requires progressive reductions in the lifecycle GHG intensity of marine fuels used by ships calling at EU ports: 2% by 2025, 6% by 2030, 80% by 2050 relative to a 2020 baseline. This creates an immediate commercial market for low-carbon fuels on transatlantic and European trade routes.

1.3 The Commercial Opportunity for US Industry

Biofuels currently meet less than 1% of global maritime fuel demand. Yet US Department of Energy analysis shows that corn ethanol can displace conventional marine fuels with a 61% lifecycle GHG reduction, soy biodiesel with 66%, and soy-based renewable diesel with 60%. These are among the most competitive and immediately deployable decarbonization options globally. Given that the US is the world's largest importer and second largest exporter of goods by value, the marine decarbonization market intersects every major US trade route — an enormous, largely untapped export opportunity for domestic biofuel producers.

2. Conventional and Advanced Biofuels

2.1 Corn Ethanol

Technology Profile

Ethanol produced from corn is the world's most widely produced biofuel, with the United States generating approximately 15-16 billion gallons per year from dry-mill and wet-mill facilities concentrated in the Corn Belt states of Iowa, Illinois, Nebraska, Indiana, and South Dakota. As a marine fuel, ethanol presents attractive properties: liquid at ambient conditions, established global supply chains, compatible with blended marine diesel applications or dedicated ethanol-fueled engines, and available at competitive price points. Leading marine engine manufacturers including MAN Energy Solutions and Wartsila have developed commercially deployed dual-fuel and ethanol-capable marine engines.

GHG Performance

DOE analysis demonstrates a 61% lifecycle GHG reduction for US corn ethanol versus conventional HFO. Next-generation techniques — integrating carbon capture and sequestration at ethanol plants, biogas for process energy, and precision fermentation — can push this figure toward 70-80% or carbon-negative territory. The Renewable Fuels Association (RFA) estimates that US ethanol used as marine fuel could generate sufficient compliance credits under the IMO NZF to meet annual standards through at least 2038. A marine engine manufacturer recently described ethanol adoption under the framework as a "beautiful case" given its handling benefits, growing availability, and competitive pricing.

2.2 Biodiesel

Technology Profile

Biodiesel is produced via transesterification of vegetable oils, animal fats, and waste cooking oils (UCO) with methanol, yielding fatty acid methyl esters (FAME) usable as direct substitutes or blending components for petroleum diesel and marine gas oil. Biodiesel blends from B10 to B30 have been successfully trialed in marine applications, including B30 blends of UCO and waste materials trialed by BP and Maersk Tankers in 2020, and B25 blends from vegetable oils commercially delivered by ExxonMobil in 2022. Exxon estimates these blends can reduce GHG emissions by up to 40% versus conventional marine fuels; certified waste-based feedstocks achieve significantly higher reductions.

GHG Performance

DOE analysis demonstrates a 66% lifecycle GHG reduction for US soy biodiesel versus conventional marine fuels — among the highest of any commercially available marine fuel. UCO and animal-fat-based biodiesel can achieve 80-90% reductions. Under the EU FuelEU Maritime well-to-wake methodology, certified waste-based biodiesel qualifies as a low-carbon fuel generating compliance credit.

2.3 Cellulosic Ethanol

Technology Profile

Cellulosic ethanol is produced from lignocellulosic biomass — agricultural residues such as corn stover, wheat straw, and sugarcane bagasse, as well as dedicated energy crops and forestry residues. It avoids the food-versus-fuel tension of corn ethanol and offers substantially improved lifecycle GHG performance from waste-stream feedstocks. Production costs have fallen significantly, and several US facilities are at commercial or near-commercial scale, with ongoing investment.

GHG Performance

Cellulosic ethanol achieves lifecycle GHG reductions of 70-100% versus fossil fuels depending on feedstock, process energy, and CCS integration. When produced with biogenic CO2 capture, cellulosic ethanol can achieve negative carbon intensity — uniquely valuable under any progressive carbon pricing regime including the IMO NZF.

2.4 Renewable Diesel (Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil — HVO)

Technology Profile

Renewable diesel (HVO) is produced through catalytic hydrotreatment of vegetable oils, animal fats, UCO, and other lipid feedstocks, yielding paraffinic hydrocarbons chemically identical to petroleum diesel. Unlike FAME biodiesel, renewable diesel is a true drop-in fuel: usable at any blend ratio including neat (100%) in diesel engines without modification, with superior cold-flow properties and long-term storage stability. Marine renewable diesel has been commercially deployed via Neste, Shell, ExxonMobil, and others at ports including Singapore, Rotterdam, and US Gulf Coast facilities. The US has 22 operational renewable diesel facilities as of early 2025, with 20 more in development or construction.

GHG Performance

DOE analysis shows a 60% GHG reduction for soy-based renewable diesel; waste and residue feedstocks (UCO, tallow, distillers corn oil) achieve 70-85% reductions. Neste estimates up to 90% lifecycle GHG reduction for its MY Renewable Diesel from waste feedstocks. Under the IMO NZF and EU FuelEU well-to-wake methodology, certified renewable diesel qualifies for strong compliance credit.

3. Green and Low-Carbon Hydrogen

3.1 Technology Overview and Marine Application

Hydrogen used in a fuel cell or combustion engine produces only water vapor as exhaust, making it inherently zero-emission at point of use. For maritime applications, hydrogen is being explored in two modalities: direct combustion in adapted marine engines (tested by MAN Energy Solutions and Wartsila) and use in PEM or solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) systems for electric propulsion. The American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) has been a global leader in defining safety frameworks for hydrogen-powered vessels, outlining a three-phase maritime decarbonization roadmap: energy efficiency in the near term, methanol and ammonia in the medium term, and deep hydrogen integration long term.

Hydrogen's low volumetric energy density — even in liquid form at -253 Celsius — presents significant storage challenges for long-range ocean-going vessels. These factors presently limit hydrogen to shorter-range ferry and coastal vessel applications, where several commercial hydrogen-powered vessels are already in service on Norwegian ferry routes. Twelve additional hydrogen-fueled vessel orders were placed in 2024 according to Lloyd's Register.

3.2 Green vs. Blue Hydrogen

Green hydrogen is produced via electrolysis of water using renewable electricity, achieving near-zero lifecycle emissions. Blue hydrogen is produced from natural gas steam methane reforming with integrated CCS, reducing lifecycle emissions by 55-70% versus unabated SMR. Blue hydrogen offers lower capital costs and faster development timescales, making it an important bridge fuel.

US hydrogen investment has been impacted by policy changes: the 45V Clean Hydrogen Production Tax Credit was materially restricted under legislation signed July 4, 2025, now available only for projects commencing construction before end of 2027. Green hydrogen remains 2-3 times more expensive than conventional marine fuels on an energy-equivalent basis, though BloombergNEF projects substantial cost declines by 2030.

4. Green and Low-Carbon Ammonia

4.1 Why Ammonia for Shipping

Ammonia (NH3) has emerged as one of the most strategically important long-term zero-emission maritime fuels. It contains 17.6% hydrogen by weight, has a volumetric energy density roughly twice that of liquid hydrogen, can be liquefied at -33 Celsius (far less demanding than -253 Celsius for liquid hydrogen), and leverages decades of global ammonia production, storage, and logistics infrastructure developed for the fertilizer industry. When burned in a marine engine or converted via fuel cell, ammonia produces no CO2. Green ammonia — produced from green hydrogen via the Haber-Bosch process — achieves zero lifecycle emissions.

4.2 Current State of Development

In March 2025, NYK Line completed a landmark three-month demonstration voyage of the Sakigake, the world's first commercial vessel retrofitted to run on ammonia fuel, achieving approximately 95% GHG reduction versus conventional fuels. MAN Energy Solutions has commercially deployed two-stroke ammonia-fueled marine engines, with multiple container ships on order. Ammonia-fueled vessel orders more than doubled in 2024, reaching 22 vessels globally. The IMO's MEPC approved interim guidelines for ammonia as marine fuel safety procedures in December 2024 — a critical regulatory milestone. DNV projects ammonia and hydrogen together could supply up to 60% of shipping fuel by 2050 under ambitious decarbonization scenarios.

4.3 Cost Profile and US Competitive Position

Green ammonia is currently projected at $885-$1,050 per tonne — roughly two to four times the cost of VLSFO on an energy-equivalent basis. Blue ammonia, produced with CCS-integrated SMR, is cheaper and is progressing to final investment decision at higher rates than green projects in the current policy environment. The US Gulf Coast holds strategic advantages: world-class natural gas feedstock (for blue ammonia), expanding renewable electricity (for green ammonia), deep geological sequestration resources, and existing large-scale ammonia production and export terminals at Houston, Corpus Christi, and New Orleans.

5. Methanol, Bio-Methanol, and E-Methanol

5.1 Methanol's Lead Position in Alternative Marine Fuels

Methanol has emerged as the leading alternative marine fuel by order volume. Leading shipping companies Maersk and CMA CGM have cumulatively ordered over 100 methanol-fueled vessels. Lloyd's Register recorded 119 methanol-fueled vessel orders in 2024 alone, adding more than a third to the existing orderbook. The first commercially operating methanol-fueled container ships are already at sea.

Methanol's commercial success derives from practical advantages: liquid at ambient temperature and pressure, stored and handled similarly to conventional fuels with modest infrastructure upgrades, established global production and logistics networks, and producible from multiple feedstocks ranging from natural gas (grey methanol) to biomass (bio-methanol) to green hydrogen and captured CO2 (e-methanol). The IMO has specified three methanol grades for marine fuel — MMA, MMB, and MMC — providing regulatory clarity.

5.2 Bio-Methanol

Bio-methanol is produced from gasification or anaerobic digestion of biomass, agricultural waste, municipal solid waste, or black liquor from paper mills. It achieves lifecycle GHG reductions of 60-95% depending on feedstock and process energy. US companies have significant advantages in bio-methanol given abundant waste biomass resources and existing chemical manufacturing expertise.

5.3 E-Methanol

E-methanol (electro-methanol) is synthesized from green hydrogen and captured CO2 — from direct air capture, industrial point sources, or biogenic sources. It achieves near-zero or negative lifecycle emissions when renewable electricity and biogenic or DAC CO2 are used. The global e-methanol market is expected to reach $1.3 billion in 2025, growing at 32.2% CAGR to $16.1 billion by 2034, driven by maritime demand. Current production costs are estimated at 469% above VLSFO, underscoring the need for green hydrogen cost reduction and carbon pricing to drive commercialization.

6. Bio-LNG and Biomethane

6.1 The LNG Fleet as Bio-LNG Ready Infrastructure

Liquefied natural gas became the dominant alternative marine fuel of the 2010s, with a global LNG-fueled fleet exceeding 1,000 vessels in service and on order. LNG reduces SOx by approximately 99%, NOx by roughly 85%, and CO2 by 20-25% versus HFO. However, methane slip — unburned methane released during combustion and fuel handling — can offset much of LNG's CO2 benefit given methane's warming potential 80 times that of CO2 over 20 years. More importantly, LNG as a fossil fuel cannot achieve the deep decarbonization required under the IMO's 2050 target.

6.2 Bio-LNG: Drop-in Zero-Carbon Fuel for the LNG Fleet

Bio-LNG is liquefied biomethane (LBM) produced from the anaerobic digestion of organic wastes — agricultural residues, food waste, wastewater sludge, municipal solid waste, and forestry residues — and liquefied to LNG specifications. Because the feedstock carbon is biogenic, bio-LNG achieves lifecycle GHG reductions of 80-100% versus conventional LNG and HFO. Bio-LNG is fully drop-in compatible with the existing LNG-fueled fleet: all 1,000+ LNG-ready vessels can switch to bio-LNG without engine modification, giving bio-LNG an enormous installed-base advantage.

The US generates vast quantities of organic waste suitable for biomethane production. The American biogas industry is among the world's most developed, with agricultural, landfill, and wastewater-treatment biogas production expanding under IRA support for renewable natural gas (RNG). Agricultural states with intensive livestock operations — Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, North Carolina, North Dakota — have methane-rich manures ideal for RNG production.

7. E-Ammonia

7.1 E-Ammonia as the Long-Run Scale Solution

E-ammonia uses the same Haber-Bosch synthesis as conventional ammonia but substitutes green hydrogen (from renewable-powered electrolysis) for fossil-derived hydrogen. The nitrogen feedstock comes from air separation, requiring no CO2 input (unlike e-methanol). E-ammonia therefore carries the GHG profile of its hydrogen input: near-zero lifecycle emissions when green hydrogen is used. Unlike e-methanol, e-ammonia does not require a CO2 supply chain, making it potentially more scalable for large-volume marine fuel use.

7.2 US Infrastructure Advantage

The US Gulf Coast is home to the world's most concentrated cluster of ammonia production and export facilities, originally built for the fertilizer industry. CF Industries, Nutrien, and OCI operate large-scale plants and export terminals at Houston, Corpus Christi, and New Orleans — ideal infrastructure for pivoting to e-ammonia export for marine fuel. Electrolysis capacity is growing across the US, though the restriction of the 45V tax credit under legislation signed July 2025 has forced project reassessment, creating urgency for near-term final investment decisions on projects that can access the full credit before the end-of-2027 construction start deadline.

8. Carbon Capture in the Marine Sector

8.1 Three Roles for Carbon Capture

Carbon capture technologies are relevant to marine decarbonization in three interconnected ways: point-source capture at biofuel production facilities to enhance lifecycle carbon profiles; direct air capture (DAC) and industrial CO2 as feedstock for e-fuels; and onboard carbon capture and storage (OCCS) systems installed on vessels themselves.

8.2 Carbon Capture at Biofuel Plants

Corn and cellulosic ethanol plants emit large, relatively concentrated streams of biogenic CO2 from the fermentation process — among the cheapest industrial CO2 to capture at $15-40 per tonne, compared to $50-100+ per tonne for dilute flue gas. Capturing and permanently sequestering this CO2 in deep geological formations transforms ethanol into a carbon-negative fuel — a profile uniquely powerful under the IMO NZF's well-to-wake accounting. Illinois Basin geological formations offer world-class sequestration capacity directly beneath the US Corn Belt. Carbon pipeline and sequestration projects are advancing across Iowa, Illinois, and Indiana to connect ethanol plants to injection wells.

8.3 Onboard Carbon Capture and Storage (OCCS)

The IMO approved a draft regulatory work plan for onboard carbon capture and storage systems at MEPC 83 in April 2025. OCCS captures CO2 from engine exhaust gases onboard a vessel, liquefies and stores it, and offloads it at port for permanent sequestration or industrial use. Studies suggest OCCS could achieve 70-90% capture rates on HFO-burning vessels, dramatically reducing well-to-wake emissions without fuel switching. This represents a potentially enormous near-term opportunity for US carbon capture technology companies: retrofitting existing vessels — which will constitute the majority of the global fleet through 2040 — with OCCS may be cheaper than newbuilding or wholesale fuel switching, particularly for older vessels where remaining operational life does not justify new engine investment.

8.4 Direct Air Capture for E-Fuel Feedstock

DAC captures CO2 directly from ambient air and is critical for producing e-methanol, e-methane, and e-kerosene with low or zero lifecycle emissions. The US leads global DAC investment: Occidental's Stratos facility in West Texas, the world's first commercial-scale DAC plant, entered operation in 2024. DAC CO2 at scale could serve as a key feedstock for e-methanol production co-located at US export terminals, creating an integrated green fuels hub strategy.

9. Comparative Analysis: Fuel Pathways for Marine Decarbonization

The following table provides a side-by-side comparison of each fuel pathway across six dimensions critical to marine deployment: lifecycle GHG reduction potential, technology readiness level (TRL 1-9), drop-in infrastructure compatibility, cost relative to conventional HFO/VLSFO, US production capacity, and projected role in the marine transition timeline.

10. Strategic Outlook and Policy Considerations

10.1 The Three Horizons Framework

A three-horizon framework usefully organizes the US opportunity:

Horizon 1 (2025-2035) — Biofuels Dominate: The near-term window belongs to biofuels. Corn ethanol, soy biodiesel, renewable diesel, and bio-LNG are commercially available, cost-competitive, and infrastructure-compatible. They can meet IMO NZF GFI targets from 2028 onwards, generating Surplus Units for operator reward. US producers should aggressively target marine bunker supply agreements, develop marine-grade product specifications and certification pathways, and engage IMO and EU bodies to ensure favorable lifecycle accounting for US biofuel feedstocks. The EU FuelEU Maritime regulation already creates an immediate, premium-price market on European and transatlantic trade routes.

Horizon 2 (2035-2045) — Methanol and Ammonia Ramp: As the global methanol-fueled fleet grows and ammonia-fueled vessels enter service, US producers must have bio-methanol and blue/green ammonia supply at scale. This requires front-loaded investment in production capacity, bunkering infrastructure at Gulf Coast and Pacific ports, and long-term offtake agreements with major shipping companies. Blue ammonia from US Gulf Coast producers is the most commercially ready Horizon 2 pathway; bio-methanol from US waste streams is a close second.

Horizon 3 (2045-2050) — E-Fuels and Full Decarbonization: Achieving the IMO's 2050 net-zero target requires zero-emission fuels at massive scale: e-ammonia, e-methanol, and green hydrogen. The US has unmatched renewable energy resources, large-scale geological sequestration, existing ammonia and methanol infrastructure, and world-class chemical engineering — the ingredients for global leadership. Policy certainty, particularly stable hydrogen production incentives and a consistent domestic carbon price signal, will determine whether the US captures or cedes this market to competitors.

10.2 Competitive Threats

Brazil's mature sugarcane ethanol industry is aggressively pursuing marine fuel markets. Indonesian and Malaysian palm-oil biodiesel sectors are large, though palm oil faces EU sustainability restrictions. China is investing heavily in cellulosic ethanol and SAF/marine biofuel production. Europe's advanced biofuels industry — Neste, Verbio, UPM, Clariant — is well-positioned for EU FuelEU compliance. The Trump administration's opposition to the IMO Net-Zero Framework, including threatening retaliatory tariffs against countries supporting the measure, risks excluding US biofuels from marine certification schemes if US positions on lifecycle accounting methodology are not heard at the IMO table.

10.3 Infrastructure and Bunkering Investment

For biofuels, the existing petroleum product distribution network is largely compatible with modest upgrades. For methanol, new marine-grade bunkering terminals and vessel-side fuel systems are needed at major ports. For ammonia and hydrogen, new cryogenic or pressurized storage and transfer systems are required. US Gulf Coast ports — Houston, Corpus Christi, New Orleans, Port Arthur — are ideally positioned to develop as global low-carbon marine fuel hubs given existing energy infrastructure, deep draft capabilities, and proximity to major biofuel and ammonia production. Investment in these hubs should be a national policy and commercial priority.

10.4 Lifecycle Accounting and Certification

The IMO NZF's well-to-wake lifecycle accounting methodology will determine which US fuels qualify for compliance credit and at what level. US corn ethanol's lifecycle GHG profile under GREET modeling (Argonne National Laboratory) differs from EU RED III methodologies in several respects. Active, sustained US engagement in IMO fuel certification scheme development is essential to ensure that US biofuels receive credit for their full GHG reduction potential, including soil carbon sequestration benefits, precision agriculture improvements, and CCS integration at production facilities.

11. Key US Companies: Consolidated Directory

The following provides a consolidated reference of US companies whose capabilities span the full spectrum of marine decarbonization fuel pathways. The list is illustrative rather than exhaustive.

Ammonia and E-Ammonia

Methanol, Bio-Methanol, E-Methanol

Bio-LNG and Biomethane

Carbon Capture (Point-Source, DAC, OCCS)

12. Conclusion

The global maritime industry's transition away from heavy fuel oil is no longer a question of if but of when — and with what fuels. The IMO Net-Zero Framework establishes the regulatory architecture for mandatory emissions reduction, making shipping the first global industry sector with binding GHG pricing. The EU's FuelEU Maritime regulation creates an immediate, premium-price commercial demand signal on European and transatlantic routes. And a growing cohort of cargo owners, financial institutions, and shipping lines is committing to green supply chains ahead of regulatory mandates.

The United States biofuels industry is exceptionally well-positioned to serve this transition in the near to medium term. US corn ethanol, soy biodiesel, renewable diesel, and bio-LNG are commercially available, cost-competitive, infrastructure-compatible, and demonstrably low-carbon. The DOE's own analysis confirms GHG reductions of 60-66% for these fuels versus conventional marine fuels — reductions that generate Surplus Units and competitive advantage for shipowners that adopt them under the IMO NZF.

Looking further ahead, the US is also home to the industrial infrastructure, engineering talent, agricultural biomass base, renewable energy resources, and entrepreneurial capital needed to scale the next generation of zero-emission marine fuels. Green ammonia from Gulf Coast export hubs, e-methanol from renewable electricity and captured CO2, bio-methanol from agricultural and municipal wastes, and onboard carbon capture systems that can retrofit the existing global fleet — all are within the US industry's grasp.

The window is open, but competition from Brazil, Indonesia, China, and Europe is intensifying. The United States must engage actively with IMO lifecycle accounting standard-setting, defend its biofuel methodologies in international certification schemes, maintain stable domestic policy support for biofuel economics, and invest in the port bunkering infrastructure that will make US fuels commercially accessible to the global fleet.

For US biofuels and alternative fuels companies, the decarbonization of global maritime shipping is not a distant abstraction. It is a large, near-term, commercially credible export market — one that rewards early movers with long-term supply contracts, premium prices, and enduring strategic positioning in the clean energy economy of the coming decades.

text:
Executive Summary

The global maritime industry stands at an inflection point. Responsible for approximately 3% of global greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions — equivalent to the total annual output of Japan — international shipping faces unprecedented regulatory, commercial, and reputational pressure to decarbonize. The International Maritime Organization's (IMO) Net-Zero Framework, approved in April 2025 and targeted for entry into force in 2027-2028, will for the first time impose binding, well-to-wake GHG fuel intensity reductions on ocean-going ships above 5,000 gross tonnage, a fleet segment representing 85% of sectoral emissions.

Into this landscape, the United States biofuels industry — encompassing corn and cellulosic ethanol, soy and waste-based biodiesel, renewable diesel, and bio-LNG — brings unmatched scale, established infrastructure, and competitive cost structures. Simultaneously, a new generation of US companies in green hydrogen, low-carbon ammonia, e-methanol, e-ammonia, and carbon capture are positioning to serve the longer-term needs of a zero-emission fleet.

This monograph provides a comprehensive analysis of each fuel pathway's technological profile, GHG reduction potential, infrastructure readiness, and cost competitiveness. It profiles the leading US companies that could supply the global marine industry. It argues that the near-to-medium term opportunity — through at least 2038 — belongs principally to biofuels, which offer proven emission reductions of 60-90%, drop-in compatibility with existing engines and infrastructure, and commercially competitive pricing. The longer-term, post-2035 transition will require massive scaling of e-fuels and green ammonia, for which US producers are investing now. Carbon capture serves as a bridge and accelerant across all time horizons.

1. The Maritime Decarbonization Imperative

1.1 Scale of the Challenge

International shipping moves approximately 90% of world trade by volume, carrying everything from raw materials and foodstuffs to finished goods and energy commodities. The industry has historically been one of the least regulated large emitters, benefiting from cheap, energy-dense heavy fuel oil (HFO) — among the dirtiest refined petroleum products. HFO's low cost has been a cornerstone of global trade competitiveness, but its environmental costs are stark: high sulfur content, fine particulate matter, black carbon, and significant CO2, methane, and nitrous oxide emissions.

The maritime sector currently consumes roughly 300 million tonnes of fuel annually, generating approximately 1 billion tonnes of CO2 equivalent each year. Without intervention, these emissions are projected to grow substantially by 2050 as global trade volumes expand.

1.2 The IMO Regulatory Architecture

The IMO has constructed an increasingly ambitious regulatory scaffold. Energy Efficiency Design Index (EEDI) requirements for new ships have been in place since 2013. Carbon Intensity Indicators (CII) and the Energy Efficiency Existing Ship Index (EEXI) entered mandatory effect in January 2023. The pivotal step came in July 2023 when MEPC 80 adopted the revised IMO GHG Strategy: net-zero emissions "by or around 2050," with checkpoint targets of at least 20-30% total GHG reduction by 2030 and 70% by 2040 versus 2008 baselines. Zero- or near-zero-emission fuels must supply at least 5% — striving for 10% — of shipping energy by 2030.

This strategy was translated into binding regulation at MEPC 83 in April 2025, where the IMO approved the Net-Zero Framework (NZF). The NZF establishes two interlocking instruments: a GHG Fuel Intensity (GFI) standard measured on a well-to-wake lifecycle basis in gCO2eq/MJ, ratcheting down annually from a 2028 baseline; and a financial compliance mechanism where ships exceeding GFI thresholds purchase Remedial Units at $100/tonne CO2eq (Tier 1) or $380/tonne CO2eq (Tier 2 for higher emitters). Ships that outperform the direct compliance target earn tradeable Surplus Units. Following disagreements at the October 2025 extraordinary MEPC session, formal adoption was deferred to 2026, with entry into force anticipated in 2027 and compliance beginning January 1, 2028.

The EU's FuelEU Maritime regulation, which entered force in January 2025, requires progressive reductions in the lifecycle GHG intensity of marine fuels used by ships calling at EU ports: 2% by 2025, 6% by 2030, 80% by 2050 relative to a 2020 baseline. This creates an immediate commercial market for low-carbon fuels on transatlantic and European trade routes.

1.3 The Commercial Opportunity for US Industry

Biofuels currently meet less than 1% of global maritime fuel demand. Yet US Department of Energy analysis shows that corn ethanol can displace conventional marine fuels with a 61% lifecycle GHG reduction, soy biodiesel with 66%, and soy-based renewable diesel with 60%. These are among the most competitive and immediately deployable decarbonization options globally. Given that the US is the world's largest importer and second largest exporter of goods by value, the marine decarbonization market intersects every major US trade route — an enormous, largely untapped export opportunity for domestic biofuel producers.

2. Conventional and Advanced Biofuels

2.1 Corn Ethanol

Technology Profile

Ethanol produced from corn is the world's most widely produced biofuel, with the United States generating approximately 15-16 billion gallons per year from dry-mill and wet-mill facilities concentrated in the Corn Belt states of Iowa, Illinois, Nebraska, Indiana, and South Dakota. As a marine fuel, ethanol presents attractive properties: liquid at ambient conditions, established global supply chains, compatible with blended marine diesel applications or dedicated ethanol-fueled engines, and available at competitive price points. Leading marine engine manufacturers including MAN Energy Solutions and Wartsila have developed commercially deployed dual-fuel and ethanol-capable marine engines.

GHG Performance

DOE analysis demonstrates a 61% lifecycle GHG reduction for US corn ethanol versus conventional HFO. Next-generation techniques — integrating carbon capture and sequestration at ethanol plants, biogas for process energy, and precision fermentation — can push this figure toward 70-80% or carbon-negative territory. The Renewable Fuels Association (RFA) estimates that US ethanol used as marine fuel could generate sufficient compliance credits under the IMO NZF to meet annual standards through at least 2038. A marine engine manufacturer recently described ethanol adoption under the framework as a "beautiful case" given its handling benefits, growing availability, and competitive pricing.

2.2 Biodiesel

Technology Profile

Biodiesel is produced via transesterification of vegetable oils, animal fats, and waste cooking oils (UCO) with methanol, yielding fatty acid methyl esters (FAME) usable as direct substitutes or blending components for petroleum diesel and marine gas oil. Biodiesel blends from B10 to B30 have been successfully trialed in marine applications, including B30 blends of UCO and waste materials trialed by BP and Maersk Tankers in 2020, and B25 blends from vegetable oils commercially delivered by ExxonMobil in 2022. Exxon estimates these blends can reduce GHG emissions by up to 40% versus conventional marine fuels; certified waste-based feedstocks achieve significantly higher reductions.

GHG Performance

DOE analysis demonstrates a 66% lifecycle GHG reduction for US soy biodiesel versus conventional marine fuels — among the highest of any commercially available marine fuel. UCO and animal-fat-based biodiesel can achieve 80-90% reductions. Under the EU FuelEU Maritime well-to-wake methodology, certified waste-based biodiesel qualifies as a low-carbon fuel generating compliance credit.

2.3 Cellulosic Ethanol

Technology Profile

Cellulosic ethanol is produced from lignocellulosic biomass — agricultural residues such as corn stover, wheat straw, and sugarcane bagasse, as well as dedicated energy crops and forestry residues. It avoids the food-versus-fuel tension of corn ethanol and offers substantially improved lifecycle GHG performance from waste-stream feedstocks. Production costs have fallen significantly, and several US facilities are at commercial or near-commercial scale, with ongoing investment.

GHG Performance

Cellulosic ethanol achieves lifecycle GHG reductions of 70-100% versus fossil fuels depending on feedstock, process energy, and CCS integration. When produced with biogenic CO2 capture, cellulosic ethanol can achieve negative carbon intensity — uniquely valuable under any progressive carbon pricing regime including the IMO NZF.

2.4 Renewable Diesel (Hydrotreated Vegetable Oil — HVO)

Technology Profile

Renewable diesel (HVO) is produced through catalytic hydrotreatment of vegetable oils, animal fats, UCO, and other lipid feedstocks, yielding paraffinic hydrocarbons chemically identical to petroleum diesel. Unlike FAME biodiesel, renewable diesel is a true drop-in fuel: usable at any blend ratio including neat (100%) in diesel engines without modification, with superior cold-flow properties and long-term storage stability. Marine renewable diesel has been commercially deployed via Neste, Shell, ExxonMobil, and others at ports including Singapore, Rotterdam, and US Gulf Coast facilities. The US has 22 operational renewable diesel facilities as of early 2025, with 20 more in development or construction.

GHG Performance

DOE analysis shows a 60% GHG reduction for soy-based renewable diesel; waste and residue feedstocks (UCO, tallow, distillers corn oil) achieve 70-85% reductions. Neste estimates up to 90% lifecycle GHG reduction for its MY Renewable Diesel from waste feedstocks. Under the IMO NZF and EU FuelEU well-to-wake methodology, certified renewable diesel qualifies for strong compliance credit.

3.1 Technology Overview and Marine Application

Hydrogen used in a fuel cell or combustion engine produces only water vapor as exhaust, making it inherently zero-emission at point of use. For maritime applications, hydrogen is being explored in two modalities: direct combustion in adapted marine engines (tested by MAN Energy Solutions and Wartsila) and use in PEM or solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC) systems for electric propulsion. The American Bureau of Shipping (ABS) has been a global leader in defining safety frameworks for hydrogen-powered vessels, outlining a three-phase maritime decarbonization roadmap: energy efficiency in the near term, methanol and ammonia in the medium term, and deep hydrogen integration long term.

Hydrogen's low volumetric energy density — even in liquid form at -253 Celsius — presents significant storage challenges for long-range ocean-going vessels. These factors presently limit hydrogen to shorter-range ferry and coastal vessel applications, where several commercial hydrogen-powered vessels are already in service on Norwegian ferry routes. Twelve additional hydrogen-fueled vessel orders were placed in 2024 according to Lloyd's Register.

3.2 Green vs. Blue Hydrogen

Green hydrogen is produced via electrolysis of water using renewable electricity, achieving near-zero lifecycle emissions. Blue hydrogen is produced from natural gas steam methane reforming with integrated CCS, reducing lifecycle emissions by 55-70% versus unabated SMR. Blue hydrogen offers lower capital costs and faster development timescales, making it an important bridge fuel.

US hydrogen investment has been impacted by policy changes: the 45V Clean Hydrogen Production Tax Credit was materially restricted under legislation signed July 4, 2025, now available only for projects commencing construction before end of 2027. Green hydrogen remains 2-3 times more expensive than conventional marine fuels on an energy-equivalent basis, though BloombergNEF projects substantial cost declines by 2030.

4. Green and Low-Carbon Ammonia

4.1 Why Ammonia for Shipping

Ammonia (NH3) has emerged as one of the most strategically important long-term zero-emission maritime fuels. It contains 17.6% hydrogen by weight, has a volumetric energy density roughly twice that of liquid hydrogen, can be liquefied at -33 Celsius (far less demanding than -253 Celsius for liquid hydrogen), and leverages decades of global ammonia production, storage, and logistics infrastructure developed for the fertilizer industry. When burned in a marine engine or converted via fuel cell, ammonia produces no CO2. Green ammonia — produced from green hydrogen via the Haber-Bosch process — achieves zero lifecycle emissions.

4.2 Current State of Development

Ammonia-fueled vessel orders more than doubled in 2024, reaching 22 vessels globally. The IMO's MEPC approved interim guidelines for ammonia as marine fuel safety procedures in December 2024 — a critical regulatory milestone. DNV projects ammonia and hydrogen together could supply up to 60% of shipping fuel by 2050 under ambitious decarbonization scenarios.

4.3 Cost Profile and US Competitive Position

Green ammonia is currently projected at $885-$1,050 per tonne — roughly two to four times the cost of VLSFO on an energy-equivalent basis. Blue ammonia, produced with CCS-integrated SMR, is cheaper and is progressing to final investment decision at higher rates than green projects in the current policy environment. The US Gulf Coast holds strategic advantages: world-class natural gas feedstock (for blue ammonia), expanding renewable electricity (for green ammonia), deep geological sequestration resources, and existing large-scale ammonia production and export terminals at Houston, Corpus Christi, and New Orleans.

5.1 Methanol's Lead Position in Alternative Marine Fuels

The first commercially operating methanol-fueled container ships are already at sea.

Methanol's commercial success derives from practical advantages: liquid at ambient temperature and pressure, stored and handled similarly to conventional fuels with modest infrastructure upgrades, established global production and logistics networks, and producible from multiple feedstocks ranging from natural gas (grey methanol) to biomass (bio-methanol) to green hydrogen and captured CO2 (e-methanol). The IMO has specified three methanol grades for marine fuel — MMA, MMB, and MMC — providing regulatory clarity.

5.2 Bio-Methanol

Bio-methanol is produced from gasification or anaerobic digestion of biomass, agricultural waste, municipal solid waste, or black liquor from paper mills. It achieves lifecycle GHG reductions of 60-95% depending on feedstock and process energy. US companies have significant advantages in bio-methanol given abundant waste biomass resources and existing chemical manufacturing expertise.

5.3 E-Methanol

E-methanol (electro-methanol) is synthesized from green hydrogen and captured CO2 — from direct air capture, industrial point sources, or biogenic sources. It achieves near-zero or negative lifecycle emissions when renewable electricity and biogenic or DAC CO2 are used. The global e-methanol market is expected to reach $1.3 billion in 2025, growing at 32.2% CAGR to $16.1 billion by 2034, driven by maritime demand. Current production costs are estimated at 469% above VLSFO, underscoring the need for green hydrogen cost reduction and carbon pricing to drive commercialization.

6.1 The LNG Fleet as Bio-LNG Ready Infrastructure

LNG reduces SOx by approximately 99%, NOx by roughly 85%, and CO2 by 20-25% versus HFO. More importantly, LNG as a fossil fuel cannot achieve the deep decarbonization required under the IMO's 2050 target.

Because the feedstock carbon is biogenic, bio-LNG achieves lifecycle GHG reductions of 80-100% versus conventional LNG and HFO. Horizon 3 (2045-2050) — E-Fuels and Full Decarbonization: Achieving the IMO's 2050 net-zero target requires zero-emission fuels at massive scale: e-ammonia, e-methanol, and green hydrogen. The US has unmatched renewable energy resources, large-scale geological sequestration, existing ammonia and methanol infrastructure, and world-class chemical engineering — the ingredients for global leadership. Policy certainty, particularly stable hydrogen production incentives and a consistent domestic carbon price signal, will determine whether the US captures or cedes this market to competitors.

10.2 Competitive Threats

Brazil's mature sugarcane ethanol industry is aggressively pursuing marine fuel markets. Indonesian and Malaysian palm-oil biodiesel sectors are large, though palm oil faces EU sustainability restrictions. China is investing heavily in cellulosic ethanol and SAF/marine biofuel production. Europe's advanced biofuels industry — Neste, Verbio, UPM, Clariant — is well-positioned for EU FuelEU compliance. The Trump administration's opposition to the IMO Net-Zero Framework, including threatening retaliatory tariffs against countries supporting the measure, risks excluding US biofuels from marine certification schemes if US positions on lifecycle accounting methodology are not heard at the IMO table.

10.3 Infrastructure and Bunkering Investment

For biofuels, the existing petroleum product distribution network is largely compatible with modest upgrades. For methanol, new marine-grade bunkering terminals and vessel-side fuel systems are needed at major ports. For ammonia and hydrogen, new cryogenic or pressurized storage and transfer systems are required. US Gulf Coast ports — Houston, Corpus Christi, New Orleans, Port Arthur — are ideally positioned to develop as global low-carbon marine fuel hubs given existing energy infrastructure, deep draft capabilities, and proximity to major biofuel and ammonia production. Investment in these hubs should be a national policy and commercial priority.

10.4 Lifecycle Accounting and Certification

The IMO NZF's well-to-wake lifecycle accounting methodology will determine which US fuels qualify for compliance credit and at what level. US corn ethanol's lifecycle GHG profile under GREET modeling (Argonne National Laboratory) differs from EU RED III methodologies in several respects. Active, sustained US engagement in IMO fuel certification scheme development is essential to ensure that US biofuels receive credit for their full GHG reduction potential, including soil carbon sequestration benefits, precision agriculture improvements, and CCS integration at production facilities.

11. Key US Companies: Consolidated Directory

The following provides a consolidated reference of US companies whose capabilities span the full spectrum of marine decarbonization fuel pathways. The list is illustrative rather than exhaustive.

Ethanol (Corn and Cellulosic)

Biodiesel and Renewable Diesel

Hydrogen (Green and Blue)

Ammonia and E-Ammonia

Methanol, Bio-Methanol, E-Methanol

Bio-LNG and Biomethane

Carbon Capture (Point-Source, DAC, OCCS)

12. Conclusion

The global maritime industry's transition away from heavy fuel oil is no longer a question of if but of when — and with what fuels. The IMO Net-Zero Framework establishes the regulatory architecture for mandatory emissions reduction, making shipping the first global industry sector with binding GHG pricing. The EU's FuelEU Maritime regulation creates an immediate, premium-price commercial demand signal on European and transatlantic routes. And a growing cohort of cargo owners, financial institutions, and shipping lines is committing to green supply chains ahead of regulatory mandates.

The United States biofuels industry is exceptionally well-positioned to serve this transition in the near to medium term. US corn ethanol, soy biodiesel, renewable diesel, and bio-LNG are commercially available, cost-competitive, infrastructure-compatible, and demonstrably low-carbon. The DOE's own analysis confirms GHG reductions of 60-66% for these fuels versus conventional marine fuels — reductions that generate Surplus Units and competitive advantage for shipowners that adopt them under the IMO NZF.

Looking further ahead, the US is also home to the industrial infrastructure, engineering talent, agricultural biomass base, renewable energy resources, and entrepreneurial capital needed to scale the next generation of zero-emission marine fuels. Green ammonia from Gulf Coast export hubs, e-methanol from renewable electricity and captured CO2, bio-methanol from agricultural and municipal wastes, and onboard carbon capture systems that can retrofit the existing global fleet — all are within the US industry's grasp.

The window is open, but competition from Brazil, Indonesia, China, and Europe is intensifying. The United States must engage actively with IMO lifecycle accounting standard-setting, defend its biofuel methodologies in international certification schemes, maintain stable domestic policy support for biofuel economics, and invest in the port bunkering infrastructure that will make US fuels commercially accessible to the global fleet.

For US biofuels and alternative fuels companies, the decarbonization of global maritime shipping is not a distant abstraction. It is a large, near-term, commercially credible export market — one that rewards early movers with long-term supply contracts, premium prices, and enduring strategic positioning in the clean energy economy of the coming decades.

Under the agreement, the companies will jointly study a demonstration project in Tomakomai, Japan, focused on decarbonizing maritime transport.
The study will run over a three-year period through fiscal year 2028 and will cover the design and operation of demonstration equipment to be installed on the coal carrier Pirika Moshiri Maru, which is owned by NYK and operated for Hokkaido Electric.

description:

text:
Until now, the investment case for alternative marine fuels has been driven by compliance – organized around the International Maritime Organization’s (IMO) Net-Zero Framework (NZF), and the European Union’s (EU) FuelEU Maritime regulation and emissions trading system (EU ETS) – with energy security treated as background context. The Hormuz crisis forces this to the front, opening an arguably more durable investment rationale for alternative fuels that does not depend on the survival of any regulatory regime.

The near-term market impact has been sharp but uneven. Prices for Singapore very low sulfur fuel oil (VLSFO) and low-sulfur marine gas oil (LSMGO) surged in the days following the start of the crisis, driven by supply risk repricing rather than confirmed physical shortages. Rystad Energy’s forecast projects the spike to peak around April to May this year, with LSMGO reaching well above $1,200 per tonne before gradually declining. Normalization is not expected until the middle of next year. However, even without triggering a structural shift in fuel choice, the price dislocation has made a deeper concern more visible: the reliability of conventional bunker supply itself can no longer be assumed.

The crisis also arrives at a moment of deepening regulatory uncertainty. The extraordinary Marine Environment Protection Committee (MEPC) session, which is scheduled for October this year, faces growing opposition, with the US, some major oil producers and Japan all pushing to weaken or replace the NZF. The worst-case scenario for clean fuel investment is not the absence of regulation but ambiguous regulation: a framework adopted in sufficiently diluted form that it generates ongoing uncertainty without providing the carbon-cost clarity needed to drive capital allocation. This is the context in which energy security shifts from supplementary argument to structural substitute.

The crisis reshapes the investment case selectively across individual fuel pathways. Biodiesel faces intensifying feedstock competition from sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) mandates. Compliance economics of bio-liquefied natural gas (bio-LNG) remain attractive for operators with surplus unit (SU) market access, but fleet applicability is narrow and delivery infrastructure immature. Biomethanol’s case is strengthening, anchored by China’s scale and strategic incentive, though supply constraints remain binding. E-methanol shares methanol’s engine compatibility advantages but sits at significantly higher production costs and, without regulatory support to bridge the gap, near-term scaling remains constrained despite the crisis compressing the cost differential at some ports. Ethanol is credible as an energy-security fuel on routes outside EU regulatory jurisdiction but still limited to a small segment of vessels. Ammonia remains structurally behind, requiring simultaneous policy pull and infrastructure investment that energy-security motivation alone cannot yet deliver.

The historical record offers a useful corrective to near-term pessimism. Previous energy shocks have consistently produced lasting structural change rather than temporary price spikes. The Hormuz disruption is likely to follow the same pattern, with one important distinction: alternative fuel technology is already commercially available at meaningful scale. The crisis does not immediately solve infrastructure immaturity, but it creates the political mandate and investment capital to accelerate that build faster than the pre-crisis compliance pathway would have delivered.

For shipowners, energy security can no longer be a background consideration. Voyage planning, bunkering choices and fuel-sourcing decisions now carry supply reliability risk alongside compliance cost risk. No single alternative fuel offers a universal solution, and the right pathway remains highly specific to vessel type, trade route and commercial structure. Those who move early to secure diversified and resilient fuel supply chains will be better positioned to absorb future shocks and to capture the commercial advantage that fuel flexibility increasingly represents.

Author:

Junlin Yu

Vice President, Head of Clean Shipping Solution

junlin.yu@rystadenergy.com

text:
Dar es Salaam, Tanzania — As global shipping braces for another round of high-stakes negotiations, a volatile mix of rising fuel costs, geopolitical tensions and deep political divisions is testing the fragile consensus around a proposed Net-Zero Framework (NZF) aimed at decarbonising one of the world's most polluting industries.

The talks, convened under the International Maritime Organization (IMO), come at a moment of acute uncertainty. A crisis in the Strait of Hormuz has sent oil and gas prices surging, exposing vulnerabilities in global supply chains and sharpening disagreements over how fast - and how fairly - the shipping sector should transition away from fossil fuels.

Experts speaking during an online media briefing warned that what is at stake extends far beyond maritime regulation. The outcome, they said, could determine the pace of the global energy transition, the stability of fuel markets, and whether developing countries are protected or sidelined in the shift to cleaner shipping.

"The Hormuz crisis has pushed up oil and gas prices, at least in the near term," said Tristan Smith, Professor of Energy & Transport at University College London. "Opponents of the Net Zero Framework - led by the United States and others with vested interests in LNG as a marine fuel - are effectively pushing to expand its use in shipping."

Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines

Smith warned that such a shift could have far-reaching consequences. "If LNG prices are already high, this would introduce a major new source of demand from a sector that does not currently rely on it, forcing competition with countries that depend on gas for electricity and basic energy needs. That risks driving prices even higher, benefiting major exporters like the US and Qatar, while creating significant disadvantages for importing countries and those reliant on gas-based products such as fertilisers."

At the heart of the debate is whether the NZF - first agreed in principle in 2025 - will be adopted as a comprehensive package combining emissions standards with a global pricing mechanism or whether it will be diluted under political pressure.

For many developing countries, the distinction is critical.

"The framework approved in 2025 was carefully designed as a package combining fuel standards and a pricing mechanism," said Michael Mbaru, a maritime decarbonisation expert at the Office of Kenya's Climate Special Envoy. "The pricing element is not optional - if it goes away, the whole framework goes away."

Without that financial pillar, Mbaru cautioned, the burden of transition would fall disproportionately on poorer nations. "Without it, developing countries risk facing the costs of transition without the tools to manage them, making the system less fair and less investable."

He added that fragmentation - where regions adopt separate rules - would further complicate matters. "Fragmentation would increase complexity and costs, especially for Africa, so we remain committed to a single global rulebook and are not willing to reopen the framework."

The stakes are already visible on the ground. Mbaru pointed to rising fuel prices in Kenya, where recent increases in petrol and diesel costs have rippled through the economy, underscoring how vulnerable many countries remain to fossil fuel volatility.

Beyond economics, the negotiations are also shaping up as a test of multilateralism.

Last year's IMO meeting ended in stalemate after a late intervention by the United States and its allies disrupted what had appeared to be a path toward adoption. Since then, countries have regrouped, and alliances - particularly among African nations - have strengthened.

"The US is a major disruptive factor, but this is not simply a US versus climate ambition debate," Mbaru said. "The shipping industry itself is calling for a global framework because it needs predictability and investment certainty."

Indeed, one of the most striking aspects of the current negotiations is the unusual alignment between regulators and industry.

"The shipping industry is very resilient, but it is constrained by uncertainty," said Femke Spiegelenberg of the Global Maritime Forum. "We know major changes are coming, but not when or how."

For shipowners and investors, that uncertainty translates into delayed decisions and missed opportunities. "The NZF provides the certainty and tools the industry is asking for - clear rules, a level playing field, and the ability to plan and invest," she said. "It is designed to reduce risk and enable investment, and weakening it would increase uncertainty and undermine the transition."

The industry's push for regulation marks a notable shift in a sector traditionally wary of global rules. But with billions already being invested in alternative fuels such as green ammonia and methanol, companies are increasingly seeking clarity on the direction of travel.

"I'm cautiously optimistic," said Rockford Weitz of Tufts University's Fletcher School. "When you look at global energy markets and the billions already being invested by industry, shipping is leading the transition."

Weitz pointed to growing momentum in Europe and Asia, where major players are moving toward zero-carbon fuels. "To me, the future is clear: it is a zero-carbon shipping future, even if politics creates short-term disruption."

Yet politics, he noted, remains a powerful force. "The Trump administration released its strategy and a February 2026 action plan, with a major focus on revitalising US shipbuilding," he said. "When you look at the details, it should actually support this transition - and the same applies to Saudi Arabia. Instead, ideology is getting in the way of policies that align with their own economic interests, and that's where the real opportunity lies."

The geopolitical context is also reshaping the economic calculus of decarbonisation. Rising fossil fuel prices, triggered by conflict in the Middle East, are making alternative fuels more competitive and strengthening the business case for green shipping.

Analysts say the developments could accelerate investment in renewable energy infrastructure, particularly in regions with abundant solar and wind resources. For countries in Africa, Asia and Latin America, the NZF could unlock new opportunities for green industrialisation - if it is implemented effectively.

Still, the path forward remains uncertain.

Negotiators face three broad scenarios: a renewed push to adopt the NZF as agreed; a shift toward weaker, technical-only measures favoured by some countries; or a compromise that delays decisions while seeking a new consensus.

Each carries risks.

A weakened framework could slow the transition and deepen inequalities. A fragmented system could increase costs and complexity. And further delays could erode investor confidence at a critical moment.

For now, experts agree on one point: the window for decisive action is narrowing.

The choices made in the coming weeks, they say, will reverberate far beyond the shipping lanes - shaping global trade, energy systems and climate outcomes for decades to come.

As Mbaru put it, the stakes are both immediate and long-term: ensuring that the transition away from fossil fuels is not only ambitious but also fair.

"The framework must reduce long-term exposure to fossil fuel shocks," he said, "while ensuring that countries with the least fiscal space are not left carrying the heaviest burden."
